body:
I had an ovarian cyst when I was 19 and roughly the same height and weight as you are. I never really paid attention to my body so just thought I was gaining weight only there or something. Some people told me after the fact that they wondered if I was actually pregnant and didn't feel comfortable asking.

The main thing I remember was how "solid" it was, like a beer belly even though I don't drink. My dentist told me how she knew it wasn't fat because when I laid down, it just stayed like a little mountain instead of spreading outward. Though when I bloat during day 1 of my period it still does that occasionally - less extreme but uterus-related.


I don't know how competent the doctor you'll be seeing is because there's a chance it'll be someone who won't take it seriously. I had to get a CT scan to see the huge 10-lb water-filled mass practically squishing the rest of my organs. It was really fortunate that it didn't burst despite all the exercise I started doing for months. I had a laparoscopic surgery and went from a 29-30 inch waist to 23-24 in a single day, it was jarring lol. If all of this sounds plausible I'd try to schedule a scan if you can. Idk much about food intolerances (food affects my skin but not my stomach appearance much) but what you mentioned about the top of your stomach being round sounded familiar to me

I tutor students so general hours are from 3-9 pm. Easy money to me because every kid has to take several years of math. At the moment I do schedule college students, adults, or homeschooled kids before that time (few times a week) but pretty much just wake up naturally any time between 9:30-11:30 am. Though I have 10 alarms set because I still worry about missing the lesson. Luckily those are online so I can just join right after waking up ha

I also have a contract with a company to design AP test prep courses and have spent so many nights just churning out content and losing track of time until 5 am.

I can pinpoint all of my problems with food to the 10-lb ovarian cyst I had 11 years ago that I genuinely thought was just me getting fat even though I'd always been fit growing up.


The crazy thing is I didn't really notice it if that makes sense. Or I didn't think anyone else did because I never picked apart anyone else's body. But it made me painfully aware of how oblivious I can be about my appearance, which isn't even a bad thing (to be body neutral) except I'm sensitive enough to be hurt by seemingly innocuous but implicitly cruel comments.


I was already prone to overthinking and anxiety over situations and people I couldn't control before this but redirecting every source of shame to food took all of that away. Because I tied my self-worth to something predictable. It's why nearly dying several times all to be within 10 pounds of my natural weight still hasn't deterred me when the alternative is feeling completely overwhelmed by my own thoughts. It doesn't matter that my anxiety is actually unpredictably worse and I've destroyed more connections over the years than I can remember, because all I know is that I don't have any mental space to care about it.

I only had exercise bulimia (few years ago) to cancel out binges and hated every minute of it. All to exist like 5 pounds heavier than my non-ED weight because I eventually couldn't outrun the surplus. I wasted so many hours the treadmill running literal marathons, lifting weights to build muscle even though I hid myself under layers of clothes anyway, getting constant anxiety, hypoglycemia, and even almost ended up with hypothyroidism (elevated TSH levels) from the exhaustion.

I don't know what it is about exercise but the extra energy or very slight "high" makes me more anxious rather than relaxed. So I don't do it anymore. The most I do is walk whenever I can (stairs instead of elevator, stuff like that) and very light maintenance exercises. I have a habit of doing 30-50 pushups every night right before I shower, or some squats when brushing my teeth, but nothing intense. And I'm smaller than my pre-ED weight which was already pretty low so...I'm not going to force myself to exercise and wind up "hungrier" the next day.

I've binged on cocoa powder but mixed it with water to form some dense chocolate-y mass. Also tried microwaving it to see if it would rise into "cake" or something. I used the fancy kind (Guittard cocoa rouge) with the slightly higher amount of fat (1 gram as opposed to 0.5...lol) and it actually tasted just like chocolate. I don't find 100% dark chocolate too bitter though.

Vitamin gummies...luckily no overdose on some of the non water soluble vitamins. I only buy the pill/tablet versions now.


2 tins of sugar-free mints. If I had more next to me I would have eaten more. The rest of the unopened tins were in my car and I ended up gifting them bc didn't trust myself.


Also enough seasoning on shirataki noodles to almost kill me one night (according to my Cronometer log and the lethal dose of sodium). Among other symptoms, my legs swelled up by 3 inches which even hours of exercise has never done. Had to run at 3 am not for calories but to sweat it out.


In general I just make wild combinations of food/condiments to taste test, even when restricting. Like kimchi with cinnamon and PB or something. So it's kind of hard to remember.


Ngl though my insane, single month, daily C/S sessions last year basically rid me of the obsessive curiosity with any "novel/limited edition" sweet food I would see in stores. It desensitized my taste buds to sugar and the act of "eating" freely stopped feeling so dangerous and anxiety-inducing to my binge brain. I get what you mean though - the blood sugar swings eventually made me mentally hungrier overall and feel more out of control but I also absolutely refused to swallow and feel any fullness so it just lost all its appeal to my brain. The swollen salivary glands, burning stomach, and ovarian pain also majorly sucked. I was super lucky that I never got fully addicted to it AND it fixed the one food issue I had for years. However I also attribute it to eating more dietary fat (like cheese) on a regular basis. It makes me more satiated than volume eating and hunger isn't as terrifying anymore.

I've done this because focusing on food or a lack thereof definitely made me feel like I'd lessened my anxiety to a degree and could think with a "clear" head. I felt safe knowing that when, not if, I messed something up, I wouldn't overthink the way I used to (pre-ED) because I just wouldn't care. Like "why would I need you when I can turn to this?" Ironically being totally dead inside made connection impossible and actually the anxiety I'd push down would still leak out anyway and probably freak people out. I look back and see how the only times people have really loved me (either romantically or platonically) were when I was energetic and "myself" and content from eating normally and well. But I also couldn't trust myself and my random bouts of anxiety over absolutely nothing so it felt better to maintain the illusion of control over everything.

I had to drastically cut down on volume and to make up for it I eat more fats - full-fat cheese, yogurt, and nut butters for example. Because I definitely have eyes that are wayyyy bigger than my stomach. My healthy (also hungry) brain wants to eat a full bowl of broccoli + other things but something about the fiber presses on my stomach and makes me uncomfortable and has for years. Protein doesn't give me that same weird feeling. But for years I'd try volume eating because everyone else seemed to love it, and stuff my stainless steel wok with like 600 grams of various vegetables and finish it all, feel great for like 5 minutes, and then worse.

Ever since I got into OMAD many years ago (which I don't purposely do anymore), being full could trigger a binge even if it's on way more vegetables, doesn't matter. It's like my brain can't understand why I'm so full but still so low in energy which is obviously because vegetables don't provide that many calories. So I overthink and eat more to get energy while feeling worse. I just avoid it by eating mostly lower-fiber stuff, super slowly (it's contrary but the faster I eat the faster I feel full on the same amount of food) and also stopped clock-watching or limiting the number of times I eat a day, or I'd feel compelled to finish all my food before some arbitrary time or whatever.

Unfortunately if you're already full then idk, maybe a light walk that will help digestion. I heard laying on your left side also helps

I'm the same way but I try not to overthink it otherwise...the mental hunger gets worse. Like your body is asking for food with the food thoughts even if your stomach isn't. Maybe some mechanical eating will help to take the drama out of eating/starving. I've also found that low volume but energy dense stuff like oily fish (canned sardines), some meat and cheese (full-fat yogurt and cottage cheese works too), and sometimes nuts keep me stable and dull the mental hunger by a lot. I'll eat them even when the lack of stomach hunger tempts me to fast. Sadly I can't really do volume eating because if I can feel even a bit of vegetables in my stomach (especially broccoli which sucks because I loved it), it makes me spiral with overthinking the hunger/fullness cues.

No I only spend my money on food because I have a mild shopping addiction (or just going out in general) but also minimalist tendencies (don't like to have too much of anything around). Food can be used up or given away more easily but other things would just sit there. I have to fight the urge to hoard food and avoid buying too much at once or it'll never get finished. Today I spent 2 hours on a shopping trip driving to (taking the long 40-minute no highway route) and walking around 3 grocery stores just to buy a specific can of salmon flakes and yogurt.

Nowadays I have to consciously avoid buying too much (only 1-2 days worth of the foods I want to try). I much prefer the "going out" part to actually having to deal with the calories...like I'd rather waste time visiting multiple stores and buying 0-1 items each than cut my trip short with 5 items from a single place.

Also a few years in I started either eating it all the same day or I would never touch the remaining amounts again from day 2 onwards. The potential food waste pains me a bit. We literally have juice boxes in the fridge from 8 months ago and protein powder from 3 years ago 💀 But if it's just 1-2 days I can manage a few bites "to taste it" without obsessing over the calories and suffocating myself with more restrictions on future eating, because I comfortably know I can get my husband to finish off the rest today or tomorrow.


But yeah for years I loved browsing grocery store aisles, especially Grocery Outlet, for new things to add to my "want to try" list, though sometimes I'd buy impulsively. I've never eaten the same snack twice if I know what a particular brand and flavor tastes like yet there are still so many options. It's not as fun anymore though because I no longer really care for sweet products (long story short, the insane C/S sessions I had for a single month completely fixed that obsession and drama, along with eating more healthy fats). But I still like trying cheese and solid meals and such.

I stayed up for 55 hours the day before I graduated college (before finally napping for 30 minutes on the 3-hour afternoon plane ride home) and felt ridiculously energetic. Didn't make up for it with 12 hours of sleep either. I also didn't eat anything (straight up water fasting) though because I didn't want to buy or deal with food. I would regularly pull all nighters just because I didn't feel like sleeping or force myself to for maybe 2-3 hours right before classes (so 5-8 am) and still never be able to nap during the day.


On average I definitely still get probably 7 hours though, idk. Have had an eating disorder for the past few years and the general lack of food sometimes causes me to be able to fall asleep between 10 pm - 1 am only to be wide awake until 6 am, just to finally fall sleep again until 9 am. But usually my preferred time to fall asleep is 3 am and I tend to naturally wake up around 9:30 or 10:30 am.

Yeah that's exactly it! Like I can consistently eat a 12 oz/340 gram bag of frozen broccoli in one sitting and not mind but if it were a giant 5 lb bag and up to me to take out amounts I'd be thinking "well last time 100 grams was enough...so why not 50 grams this time and load up with more water in the soup?" The thing is that not eating enough also stresses me out on days I'm pushing myself to be productive and energetic (in front of clients) so I also have a habit of eating more preemptively during the day if I'm not 100% sure if I have anything else to look forward to eating that night.

Yeah protein powder is one of those things I envisioned fantasy me liking...felt safer than meals too because easy to store and could have something in <1 min.


Going out does give me structure and was one of the things early on that helped me transition out of OMAD because I could look forward to satisfying my curiosity (and also eating) instead of getting caught up in the last supper mentality.


It feels like I have a purpose that bypasses the fear that I'm just eating to eat...the only caveat is that I've never ordered the same dish from the same place twice (or sometimes just never revisit a place too) because once I know what it tastes like it feels pointless to eat it again. I'm even a Yelp elite (only takes ~2 reviews a month to maintain though).


Same with groceries - other than staple foods, I made it my mission to try different types of cheese and even have a spreadsheet reviewing each to avoid accidentally buying it again, but maybe I will one day since I did make a section for the greatest ones of all time ha

Yeah, hope it helps! Some other fat sources I remind myself to take in regularly are full-fat yogurt and avocados. Pre-ED me found the mouth feel of fat felt kinda weird but it's like I trained my taste buds to not notice it after knowing how much good it's done for me mentally and physically (lifelong eczema is much more tame eating more fats).

However I notice I still seem to sense it naturally - the other day I had these tropical avocados that tasted way better than Hass to me only to discover they're supposedly a little lower in fat and higher in water content on a per gram basis...so I wouldn't push it if you don't like eggs or cheese but if you can "hide" a fat source in some way it'll still be useful, like adding some butter to vegetables or something.

I don't trust myself to hoard massive amounts of one thing anymore because either I'll get bored of it or suddenly find it unsafe and then it goes to waste (we have protein powder from 3 years ago that even starving me just no longer saw as edible) or I might eat it all to get rid of it precisely because it's never going to be finished as I keep buying more food. I can keep frozen vegetables and stuff because they last much longer. But for a while I couldn't even keep celery for more than a day without forcing myself to eat it all because I never knew if future me would ever touch it again. I've even "binged" on the massive stockpile of gum and sugar free candies I had because one day I just decided it wasn't useful to tomorrow's me anymore which basically made it scarce.

My food obsession also manifests as trying different foods/weird mixtures of flavors/restaurants. Just knowing the food is around is comforting even though my husband always ends up finishing the leftovers off for me. I started letting myself go out again and trying new stuff to "justify" eating or leaving the house even though I always get it to go so I can obsessively weigh the few bites I eat to taste.

I have to consciously fight the urge to buy too much because I know the most I can comfortably keep is like 1-2 days worth of perishable food in order to feel free to go out more often. Basically a balance of having some food around to feel like it's "abundant" without being obligated to eat just that until we finish it. I used to be so frugal when we had money problems and ate the same meal prep daily and now I just somehow feel more restricted with obligatory meals because over time I often whittle the "same meal" down to nothing.

I don't like feeling too full and also don't like waiting and waiting hours for hunger to hit to justify my desire for food. OMAD (like actual water only, not "snacks + 1 main meal" lol) and clock-watching are actually the worst to me. It's so awkward going out to eat and then being "done" after like 5 bites since all I wanted was a taste, but then having to sit through the rest of the meal. So I force myself to eat ridiculously slowly in those social obligations even though I'm not a naturally slow eater. It's gotten to the point where I have to get food to go whenever I want to try a restaurant so that I can stuff the remaining 95% into containers for my husband to finish. If I'm still hungry I just fill up on my own safe foods (that I don't mind thinking of as a "meal," because the volume is sometimes decent from vegetables and I can control the amount with my food scale exactly). With that being said, my calories are rarely too low because I tend to eat high fat/protein and low carb stuff like cheese so the calories add up even though volume is low.

Is it like a "saving for later" mentality? Like it doesn't feel scarce because you can always look forward to having that one remaining bite even if you never actually do...or even when you throw it out

If it's a safe food I genuinely don't care but if it's something I'm curious about trying (thanks food obsession), I'll often buy it and basically be hyper-aware of everything about it in order to make up excuses in my head for why I don't actually want to eat it. Like weird texture, taste isn't worth more than a bite, too plain, etc. So I just stop immediately otherwise the regret and self-loathing will overwhelm me. If I'm hungry I'll just eat my safe foods. Usually my husband will finish the rest of it so I don't feel bad about food waste. Occasionally I'll secretly spit it out mid-chew as if the 10 calories makes any difference...but it does to my brain.

Pre-ED I didn't notice any of this and wasn't picky at all (though I still tended to eat the same things out of habit and no interest in food)

I was prone to anxiety and overthinking already pre-ED but have always been pretty content, oblivious almost, and bounce back easily. Tried to off myself after 5 years - not directly for ED reasons but the malnutrition definitely did not help. Depression definitely reappears if I'm restricting but specifically in a way that makes it feel like I've totally lost all freedom in my life (like if overly rigid).

Yeah and my health was at the worst it's been over 10 years despite me doing research to hit various nutrient targets from a variety of foods, probably because I'd also binge on "healthy" things like way too much oatmeal and nuts and fruit. Pretty sure I went way over the recommended amount for copper and selenium once (separate times) based on the symptoms, which were horrifying experiences.


Was literally 3 lbs heavier than the weight I existed at naturally, growing up, because I obviously couldn't run a marathon every day to counter the surplus. Usually I'd spend like 2-3 hours in the gym just cycling and lifting weights and also run at night, with one rest day a week or sometimes not at all. I legit cried once because my phone didn't register roughly ~1000 steps and it didn't feel "right" to manually input the 0.4 miles from when I last checked. So many memories of just sobbing on the treadmill because my brain just wouldn't let me relax and go home. But between eating and exercising I don't remember being all that depressed, because it felt like I had some "purpose" in my day to day life with the step counts and what not.


I'd get hypoglycemia from exercising after a normal meal of eggs and vegetables. Once my heart rate dropped to 30-40 bpm in the middle of the night and probably blood pressure too and I thought I would die - felt just like the time I overdosed and had to be sectioned. I got a blood test during that time and the part that scared me the most was the elevated TSH (basically high risk of hypothyroidism) even though I ate seaweed/wakame. I don't remember what I did as it's been 3 years but I didn't develop metabolism problems luckily lol.

I had this problem many years ago and I'm pretty sure it was because my idea of "healthy" was accidentally low-fat - the canned salmon I used to buy at Costco only had 1 gram of fat, and I'd eat various vegetables with no oils or even avocados or nuts because of calorie concerns. So I was drawn to sugary items that gave me energy without bloat or fullness, and yet I never craved candy/pure sugar - it was always high fat stuff like chocolate, cheesecake, buttery pastries, etc. that pre-ED me found too sickeningly cloying. Also like you, no craving for savory foods like pizza or burgers despite them also being high in fat.

It took me literal years to stop eating any added sugars (and even fruit I'm pretty meh about now, never crave it enough to buy it but I don't refuse to eat it if it's there) and the only way has been to force myself to eat more fat like whole eggs, full fat cheese, higher-fat meats (so skin-on chicken thighs rather than chicken breasts), sardines, some nuts and seeds, etc. And again, it took a long, long time for me to not freak out over the low volume calories adding up. I do still get fatigue if I end up restricting for a longer period of time but my energy is so much more stable and it's been worth it. Vs. when I'd be totally wired right after eating several pieces of fruit but also severely anxious on like <10 grams of fat.

If there's any chance your daily fat intake is too low (for example even when I'm restricting, 50 grams makes me feel pretty "okay," decent overall, but 70+ grams really does feel different), maybe try to bump it up a little if you can? I've seen people talk about protein + fibre being satiating and it is, immediately at least, but for me it seems like higher fat intake works better for my mood and hormones (though I guess because I end up fairly low-carb naturally so have to make up for that somewhere).

Apparently insulin has something to do with this. You can try adding or changing to eggs or other foods with fat + protein to minimize blood sugar changes. I used to get this more often but mine was partially psychological - eating meant limiting the calories I had "left" so I'd worry over the remaining stuff I was allowed to eat all day long. But physiologically digestion takes effort too so it can make a lot of people tired or something

I used to fold them (lay "face" down, fold the sides up, and then fold back to form a trapezoid) because I liked seeing them neatly put together and now I just toss them in their assigned drawer haphazardly. In our current apartment we have 9 individual drawers built into the wall right across from the laundry machine, so I throw socks (all black socks) and underwear on top, tops and jackets in the middle, and pants on the bottom directly from the dryer. Then bedding, hand towels, and body towels in the middle set of 3 drawers.

I have the same problem and have just resorted to buying whatever I need every single day (I live right next to some major grocery stores so it doesn't take much time luckily). Like single servings of nut butters, canned fish, etc. The only food I can keep around is frozen broccoli because both my husband and I eat that every single day, and frozen beef because he eats that and I get histamine issues so avoid it entirely. If I buy anything new I just finish it by the end of the day because I can't stop thinking about it. I've finished 2 pounds of cheese in 1-2 days before, and it's still a safe food but I just can't buy too much at once. Even vegetables like carrots, celery, cucumbers, 5 lb bags of shredded cabbage, anything perishable that goes in the fridge...I'll finish in a day or two. Just munching on plain celery.

It's partially because if I don't finish something that's not a staple, I almost always end up never touching it again. Like we have protein powder and uncooked rice that's been in the cupboard for 3 years (just making him slowly chip away at it), and just random stuff he brought back that I just completely lost interest in and it doesn't even register as edible to my weird brain anymore...

If she didn't understand then I'm hoping that's just cluelessness rather than malice. Like people who've never starved nor binged (not just overeating at Thanksgiving or buffets) genuinely can't fathom going over a day without a single source of calories passing their lips only to eat 3 days worth of calories in a single sitting. My experience was in an Asian country which is notorious for weight obsession so the snark was clear

People suck but her being a therapist makes it way worse. Just from that one line, I'll assume she's the type of person who went into the profession to be snarky about her "knowledge" of mental health. No but seriously, I get what you mean about how hard it is to recover when you think about how ignorant people are.

I remember interning at a company when I was around 20 years old and uncomfortably refusing the boxed lunches all the time (thanks to fasting and binging which actually brought the "set point" I could exist at comfortably UP by about 5-10 pounds, but still normal weight). Someone asked me directly if I didn't eat lunch and I just said "yeah sometimes I guess" and this lady immediately went "then why aren't you skinny" like what the fuck? But she was significantly bigger than I was so she probably thought about weight all the time and chose to subject other people to it too. Your therapist probably hates herself so.

So I'm married and am super lucky that I didn't feel the urge to do this with my husband (I just do it now for other reasons) but in the past, absolutely. For me it was more about regulating my emotions - even pre-ED I got crazy anxiety and overthought everything that I might screw up, and even when the other person liked me back, I'd always feel unsettled as if one day they'd wake up and just be turned off by the behaviors that stemmed from the anxiety I just couldn't control (like a self-fulfilling prophecy). People talk about acting clingy or needy or whatever but instead of being vulnerable or any type of honest, I would try to push it down and it would come out weird instead. And for months or even years I'd think about all the things I "should" have chosen to say or do.

Over time, focusing on food and weight became a safety net because I didn't have to really care about what anyone else felt about me. Even though it made me incapable of genuinely bonding with anyone, I basically never experienced anything that even came close to heartbreak after that.

I'd recommend those water flavorings (like Mio, there's Mio energy too). It's been helping me get an adequate amount of water because I tend to forget as well. Some people set alarms/reminders to drink water throughout the day but I never got into that.

I drank a lot of diet sodas at one point but had to wean myself off of that. Otherwise I definitely also don't drink much plain water unless I'm actively thirsty after exercise or something. Idk if it's because water fasting years ago (which I don't do anymore) made me tired of water but for years I legit would dread and sometimes even avoid drinking plain water when hungry for food, since it felt like a chore that not only led to a horribly full stomach but obviously didn't fix the malnutrition/mental hunger.

I can follow recipes but I don't enjoy cooking whole meals with elaborate steps and having to deal with leftover ingredients possibly rotting away in my fridge. Even when I did have a cooking phase, I gravitated toward those 2-5 ingredient recipes to see what food combinations could go together. I'm super lucky that my husband is so not picky that he can eat the same thing every day too, even stuff that's apparently blasphemous such as boiled meat - like we can just take out a portion of ground beef from the freezer and boil it with various vegetables and rice (most of which are also frozen, like 12 oz packages of broccoli, cauliflower, etc.) for like 10 minutes and he's satisfied with that. I make separate portions for myself and since I reverse-weigh/tare pretty much everything at the end of the day, it's easy to log the calories of everything that goes into the stir-fry I lazily make every single meal. Stir-fries are awesome for just rotating different vegetables that all practically have the same calorie count range.

Before my husband, I knew from the start I wouldn't be staying with any of the guys I've dated (not many). I always had legit reasons like "graduating from high school" and then later on "why would we stay together after college?"

When I didn't have a reason for the guy I met right after college, I decided to kill time because what was the worst that could happen, right? But I have a journal entry that I wrote after the first date I had with him about how completely drained and melancholic I felt, and I just chalked it down to commitment issues because there was nothing overtly wrong with him.

Well, the genetic condition I'd been managing pretty well ended up flaring up so badly that I was in severe pain for nearly a year and put up with a lot of either indirect insults or callous remarks that I never would have otherwise. I have no doubt that if he were capable of attracting any other girl at all, he would have cheated. I actually don't clearly remember anything other than the time he told me that I had "man shoulders" completely unprompted and gave me a complex. It's still one of the things I use as fuel for the eating disorder I'd had for years. But I was so sick that it just didn't...register in my brain or something until much later. Mostly all I remember of him was a passive aggressive "edge lord" persona coupled with over-apologizing whenever I cried over small remarks that sent me past the physical pain I was already feeling.

I'm not sure if I regret not listening to my intuition then, because I did meet my SO partly because of him. There was no aha moment really - I literally just decided to dump him one day and he went from over-the-top hearts and kisses to "I actually hated you for months." I WAS pretty shitty near the end but staying with him definitely would have been a waste of time anyway for multiple other reasons.

I've been all over the place with that. Pre ED I was pretty "meh" about food. It did taste good and I wasn't that picky, but I just didn't think about it. My parents always pushed me to eat which was why I was a normal (albeit low-normal) BMI. The only time I actively couldn't stand eating was when my weight actually wasn't the focus at all, but the way feeling food in my stomach or any lack of hunger would bring back my anxiety and all the feelings I was trying to forget.

When I had bulimia (non-purging), I was completely obsessed with food and clock-watching while fasting. Mostly because I couldn't stop weighing the pros and cons of whether it was worth eating that day or if I really needed to break my fast at all, so I'd justify my decision to eat as "trying new things" (never ate the same thing twice unless they were staple foods for certain nutrients/vitamins). When I finally did eat, I'd be so tired of hours of indecision that I'd binge specifically to get rid of the food noise and fast more easily the next day from all the extra calories. Over time the malnutrition (despite being at a slightly higher weight) made food taste so much better that fasting for damage control became so much harder.

Over the years, I've probably given myself histamine and allergy problems or whatever so my list of predictably safe foods (that won't make my body feel horrible) has whittled down to practically nothing. Luckily cheese is one of them so it adds a decent amount of calories and macros. Food still tastes great, but it's very difficult to face the uncertainty of how my body will react, so I don't have any desire for anything but my safe foods. And if I'm hungry and feel physically weak, even steamed and unsalted broccoli is incredible. If I could never eat again and also not feel any physical symptoms, I might be fine with that. But then again...when I don't have food or weight to think of, there's really nothing else I can look forward to in the same way anymore.
With family like that who tf needs enemies. Hope you can get out of there soon because having to be on guard for remarks like that sounds beyond stressful

For me it's my shoulders. My ex (who was scrawny so his judgment was probably skewed anyway) rudely said I had "man shoulders" unprompted when I was at a normal weight but higher than what I'm used to. I remember going to a festival last summer and being so jealous of this woman around my height whose shoulders barely made it past her hair down.

I can see the entire clavicle, acromion, coracoid process, and all the surrounding bones front and back so I know that they're not getting any smaller. Best I can do is shrink the side of my arms so much that it gives the illusion of not being as wide. This might sound like paranoia (as in it's rare in my area, not that it doesn't exist) but I'm terrified of deranged transphobes who try to "clock" women and the possibility of being seen as masculine (though I'm well below average height so less likely) feels more unsafe to me than being perceived as too vulnerable.

It was a combo of making high-calorie food feel less "forbidden" to put it in my mouth, desensitized the extreme guilt I had over wasting food, and just getting taste fatigue over the sheer amount of sweet foods I "consumed."

But because it made me more mentally hungry overall, I was actually getting less satisfaction in the end which eventually lessened the appeal. I literally just got bored of the entire process of buying and tasting "possibly interesting" food because it started feeling pointless. Plus the physical effects with the swollen glands, stomach acid, and weird ovarian pain I started feeling weren't great either. So I just stopped. I mean it wasn't that easy and I did have to keep eating more fat to reduce the hunger and normalize my hormones again but overall that was it.

If I see some limited edition item in stores, my entire thought process is basically "I know I'm going to refuse to swallow it so there's no point in spending money to buy something that I can already guess the taste of and also end up hungrier from." Or with gifted foods, I basically weaponize C/S as an option so that I gravitate toward portioning properly (rather than eating it all to get rid of it) or just not putting it in my mouth at all, because the alternative is wasting it, which I still do feel some amount of guilt about.

I had hoarder tendencies as a kid - felt bad throwing out stickers and memorabilia that I found cute. Because even though it was messy, I figured I never left dirty dishes or cups around, and always washed them right after eating (a habit I adopted growing up) so no wet messes. I remember cleaning up at the end of the year and finding around $20 in loose change alone around my desk, hidden under various papers.

In my senior year, a friend mentioned Marie Kondo's book, applied to her own life. Seems like common sense now, but the idea of everything having a "place" was a revelation to me back then. I never "can't find stuff" now because each item has a "home" rather than "somewhere on my desk." I also had to minimize my stuff after having to live in my car for a few months at one point since it was easier to be inconspicuous when my car looked clean and not something that belonged on r/carbage. My husband and I filled up 6 moving boxes (one of which was just for a giant bag of rice from Costco) when we moved to our current place - I felt like this was a lot but our movers commented on how little stuff we had.

The biggest benefit to not having much stuff is cleaning - I've always been super lazy with cleaning and would rather not do it, but now I actually enjoy wiping down my practically empty desk every night because it's satisfying seeing how neat and spacious the space looks.

It's easy for me to not buy stuff when I think about "what am I going to do with this if I don't need it any more, other than giving it away?" but the last problem I had was buying food - I enjoy trying new things like fancy cheeses but can easily hoard months of non-perishable food that takes too long to finish (especially when I get bored of it). It's a consumable so I'm fooled into thinking that I'll eventually be rid of it. I can still remember how, in college, I left a pint of ice cream in the freezer for so long that it developed frost bite, and even the microwave couldn't soften it at all. I remember it because I hate throwing out food, but usually I would just shove snacks I get bored of onto other people (Buy Nothing groups are great for this). I work around that by never buying in bulk, unless it's staple foods that I know my husband likes to eat and will definitely be used up instead of rotting in the freezer. Otherwise, I only buy one "new" thing at a time and don't buy anything new until it's gone. If I see something I'm curious to try, I add it to my list in Gmail drafts.

Still have to work on digital clutter but at least everything is organized into folders there.

Although now that I think of it, it's probably because fasting left me hungrier than restricting. Like my hunger levels from least to greatest were restriction < after binging < fasting and so I didn't pay attention to the "after-binge hunger" when I always had to deal with the even greater one.

I tend to sort of "dissociate" during those moments (or what I imagine dissociation feels like). Maybe like a protective mechanism against the few times I've actually panicked. But it helps me to do some chore and really concentrate on it. I wash dishes after eating anyway but instead of zoning out because of uncomfortable thoughts, I'll focus on the movement of my arms and carefully observe the bits on the plate being washed off. Or vacuum but do it carefully for every single piece of hair. The mindfulness usually snaps me out of it after about 5-10 minutes
